name: Choosing versus rejecting
statement: Asked which option to pick and asked which to eliminate, people are said to name the same vivid option both times, which cannot both be right.
meaning: The test needs two groups and one pair of options. One option is average on everything; the other has stronger good points and stronger bad points. Ask one group to award custody and the other to deny it. If preferences are coherent, the two percentages should add to 100: whoever you would award to is whoever you would not deny. Shafir predicted they would add to more than 100, because choosing makes you look for reasons in favour and rejecting makes you look for reasons against, and the extreme parent supplies more of both. That would mean the question's verb, not the options, decides the answer.

origin.note: The paper is "Choosing versus rejecting: Why some options are both better and worse than others", and the custody vignette is the version everyone quotes.

evidence: In the original, 170 people were split between an award group and a deny group. The award group gave custody to the extreme parent 64% of the time, and the deny group denied it to the same parent 55% of the time. The sum is 119%, and Shafir reported the excess over 100 as reliable, z = 2.48, p < .02. Many Labs 2 later converted that result to d = 0.35, with a 95% confidence interval from -0.04 to 0.68.

examples.tag: The flat with the garden and the commute
examples.text: One flat is fine on everything and a second has a large garden and an hour's travel. Asked which to take, a viewer names the second; asked which to rule out, another viewer names the second again. Both cannot be the right answer.

A panel told to pick names the candidate who is brilliant in places and weak elsewhere, because the strengths are the reasons a choice asks for. A panel told to eliminate names the same person, because the weaknesses are the reasons a rejection asks for.

examples.tag: The holiday crossed off the list
examples.text: A couple compare a reliable hotel with a resort that has a famous beach and poor food. Which verb the question uses decides which of the resort's two extremes comes to mind, and so decides the answer.

replication.headline: Across 7,901 people the two percentages summed to 93 rather than the 119 the original reported, missing the coherent 100 from the other side.
replication.detail: Many Labs 2 ran the custody vignette in the second of its two slates, which 61 samples completed. Participants awarded custody to the extreme parent 45.5% of the time and denied it 47.6% of the time. Those sum to 93%, which is reliably below 100 rather than above it, d = -0.13 with a 95% confidence interval from -0.18 to -0.09. The direction is the opposite of the prediction. Shafir's account says the extreme option should attract both the award and the denial; what happened is that the average parent did.

study.cite: Klein, R. A., Vianello, M., Hasselman, F., et al. (2018). Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(4), 443-490.

limits: One vignette, one pair of options. Shafir's paper carries eight problems, and Many Labs 2 replicated only the custody one, so this is a verdict on that demonstration rather than on the idea that selection and elimination can differ. A second team tested all eight. Chandrashekar and colleagues ran a preregistered close replication in 2021, with 1,026 people answering every problem, and their combined estimate was d = -0.01, 95% confidence interval -0.06 to 0.03. On the custody problem the two shares summed to 101.8%, the original's direction but not reliable, and their Bayes factor favoured the null by about eight to one. Two of the eight problems, both lotteries, did reproduce the original pattern. Many Labs 2 also departed from the original in a way its own table of deviations records: the two parents were not counterbalanced, and the average parent always came first. Shafir replied in the same issue, naming that fixed order and the ageing of the parents' features as possible causes of the reversal. The interval quoted above is not Shafir's. Many Labs 2 built it from cell sizes, assuming an equal split where a paper did not report them, so the estimate it produced contains zero while Shafir's own z test did not.
misreadings: The custody problem is a fixture in decision-making courses, usually presented as a demonstration that preferences are constructed by the question rather than retrieved. That lesson may still be right, but this experiment no longer supports it. The result is also sometimes described as people being inconsistent, when the replication found people more consistent than coherence requires rather than less: a sum of 93% means the two groups were converging on the same answer from both directions. Shafir's published reply is missed too. He does not concede the effect, and holds that the replication's materials and its fixed option order could produce the reversal by themselves. His reply also says Wedell replicated the original result for the item Many Labs 2 used, which Wedell's paper does not report: of the five problems Wedell modelled on Shafir's, only one moved significantly in the predicted direction, and it was not the custody one.
